questions.q: In a novel you read « Il entra dans la pièce ». Which modern tense does entra correspond to?
questions.why: The passé simple is the literary equivalent of the passé composé: a completed event that moves the story forward. Il entra reads as il est entré.

questions.q: « Il mangeait » and « il mangea » — which is which?
choices: mangeait is passé simple, mangea is imparfait
mangeait is imparfait, mangea is passé simple
questions.why: The -a ending is the passé simple of an -er verb: a narrative event. The -ait ending is the imparfait: description or habit. In a literary paragraph they alternate constantly.

questions.q: Which verb is « il vit » in a passé simple narrative? Give the infinitive.
questions.why: Vu gives vit, in the i family. Out of narrative context, il vit is also the present of vivre — only the surrounding tenses decide.

questions.q: Which verb is « il naquit » ? Give the infinitive.
questions.why: Naître gives naquit, one of the genuinely irregular stems along with venir → vint, tenir → tint, être → fut and faire → fit.

questions.q: Match them: « il fit », « il fut », « il vint ».
questions.why: Fit is faire, fut is être, vint is venir. One letter separates fit from fut, and both are extremely common in narrative.

questions.q: Which verb is « il sut » ? Give the infinitive.
questions.why: For most verbs the passé simple stem is the past participle minus its ending: su gives sut, bu gives but, voulu gives voulut, pris gives prit.

questions.q: « Nous vîmes la mer. » Who is doing what?
questions.why: Vîmes is the nous form of voir in the passé simple. The circumflex marks the nous and vous forms across all three families: parlâmes, finîmes, eûmes.

questions.q: « Je parlai » and « je parlais » differ by one letter. What is the difference in meaning?
choices: Passé simple, a single narrative event, versus imparfait, description or habit
questions.why: In practice context decides: a run of narrative events is passé simple, a background description is imparfait.

questions.q: Convert to modern French: « Ils eurent peur. » → Ils ___ peur.
questions.why: Eurent is the ils form of avoir in the passé simple, so the modern equivalent is the passé composé: ils ont eu.

questions.q: Convert to modern French: « Elle partit sans un mot. » → Elle ___ sans un mot.
questions.why: Partit is the passé simple of partir, so the passé composé with être, and the participle agrees with the feminine subject.

questions.q: « Quand il eut fini, il partit. » What is eut fini?
choices: passé antérieur — the literary counterpart of the plus-que-parfait
questions.why: Avoir or être in the passé simple plus a participle gives the passé antérieur, used after quand, dès que and après que. Modern French says quand il a eu fini or quand il avait fini.

questions.q: « Bien qu'il fût tard, elle continua. » What is fût?
choices: imperfect subjunctive of être, where modern French would say soit
questions.why: The circumflex on a third person singular is the marker: fût, eût, vînt, parlât are imperfect subjunctives. Compare il fut, no circumflex, which is the passé simple.

questions.q: « Il eût été plus simple de partir. » How should you read eût été here?
choices: as a past subjunctive: qu'il ait été
as a past conditional: il aurait été
as a passé antérieur: il eut été
as a plus-que-parfait: il avait été
questions.why: The plus-que-parfait du subjonctif doubles as a literary past conditional, sometimes called the deuxième forme du conditionnel passé. The sentence is hypothetical, so read it as aurait été.

questions.q: Type what you hear, as it would be written in a novel.
questions.why: Ouvrir belongs to the i family: ouvert gives ouvrit. Modern French would say il a ouvert la porte.

questions.q: You meet an unfamiliar verb form in a nineteenth-century novel. What three questions do you ask, and what does each answer tell you?
a: 1. Does it end in -a, -it, -ut, -irent or -urent? Then it is a passé simple — read it as a passé composé. 2. Does it carry a circumflex in the third person singular (fût, eût, vînt, parlât)? Then it is an imperfect subjunctive — read it as a present subjunctive. 3. Is it eût or fût plus a participle in a hypothetical sentence? Then read it as a past conditional. That covers essentially all of it.
questions.why: The point of the chapter is recognition, not production: three questions turn every literary form back into a tense you already use.
